A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same work. The text, equations, figure, references, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between sections and appendices.

before.justification: Section III attributes ternary-cause findings to the authors' numerical examples, but supplies only an external reference. The PDF does not clarify whether these constitute simulation results or mathematical constructions. The remaining evidence consists of proofs and literature illustrations.

after.justification: Section II-C reports an original simulation using 10 million Dirichlet-generated probability tables, estimating Simpson's paradox frequency as 4.29% ± 0.001%. Appendix B also reports the authors' processing and analysis of published smoking data.

M1.justification: Section VI adds a Gaussian latent-common-cause model and a covariance-based decision formulation for continuous variables, extending v1's discrete conditional-probability approach. The binary screening relation and associated decision rule are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds a distinct simulation task estimating paradox prevalence over Dirichlet-generated joint distributions. Smoking and COVID-19 were already represented in v1; however, v2's COVID analysis concerns ages 60–79 and 80+, replacing the earlier illustrative comparison above and below 65. The Gaussian extension is analytical, not additional empirical coverage.

E2.justification: Section II-C introduces an explicit numerical comparison with Pavlides and Perlman's homogeneous-prior and Jeffreys-prior estimates, respectively 1.66% and 2.67%. This comparison is absent from v1. Those comparator results are attributed to prior work; v2 does not establish that they were rerun.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a simulation protocol with eight joint probabilities, Dirichlet parameters of 1/8, 10 million samples, and the sign tests in Eq. (14). The COVID age stratification also changes explicitly. Newly documented smoking preprocessing does not establish that an earlier experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The brief smoking and COVID illustrations become detailed case analyses in Sections IV–V. Appendix B identifies the exceptional smoking association for ages 25–34 and examines aggregation into binary age groups. Section II-C additionally investigates whether the paradox occurs under the proposed unbiased sampling model.

E5.justification: v2 first reports numerical uncertainty, attaching ±0.001% to its 4.29% simulation estimate. It does not explain the uncertainty calculation or report seeds or repeated-run counts. The 10 million samples are a sample size, not evidence of additional independent runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds the 4.29% simulation estimate and concrete application probabilities, including smoking mortality of 0.2214 versus 0.2485 and COVID mortality of 0.0608 versus 0.0760 for China and Italy. Appendix B qualifies v1's broad smoking reversal description by identifying an age-group exception before pooling. These are new findings and entries, not performance gains under matched settings.

T1.justification: The binary theorem and matrix-inversion appendix are retained. v2 adds Gaussian covariance derivations and Theorem 2, supporting matrix identities in Appendix D, and a two-component common-cause construction in Appendix E. It also introduces necessary condition (6), which conflicts with its own COVID example.

C1.justification: The main resolution claim expands from binary variables to the minimal continuous Gaussian setting. The introduction and new Impact Statement also foreground paradox prevalence and application-specific predictions. The ternary-cause qualification disappears from the abstract but remains in Section III-C.

C2.justification: v1 describes smoking as influencing the age distribution; v2 assumes that influence is absent and proposes a genetic common cause. v2 explicitly concludes that China did worse than Italy under a binary healthcare-system cause, contrasting a published mediation interpretation. It also discusses the limitations of requiring exact screening and minimal causes.

D1.justification: v2 documents the simulation specification and, in Appendix B, smoking age-group weights, exclusion of ages 75+, and pooling procedures. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Conversely, v1's repository reference for ternary numerical examples is replaced by 'available upon request' in v2.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands engagement with decision theory, paradox-frequency estimation, continuous-variable and data-mining research, smoking genetics, and COVID mediation analysis. It also positions common-cause screening in relation to unsupervised learning and develops more specific criticism of causal-graph interpretations.

P1.justification: The introduction and literature discussion are extensively rewritten and reorganized into dedicated subsections. Several appendix examples move into the main text, the ternary discussion moves out of the summary, and the original inversion appendix becomes Appendix C. An Impact Statement and a more developed research roadmap are added.

P2.justification: The single-column presentation becomes a journal-style two-column main text and reference list, with single-column appendices. Front matter, headings, equation wrapping, and spacing are extensively reformatted. Figure 1 retains the same four causal graphs but is relocated and rescaled; no additional figures or tables are introduced.

improvement.justification: The Gaussian derivation and documented numerical analyses strengthen scope and traceability. However, new necessary condition (6) conflicts with Section V: its probabilities imply p(b|a2)=0.8983 and p(b|not a2)=0.6859, both above 1/2. Equation (16) also omits common-cause mixing weights, while numerical-example access becomes request-only. These substantive consistency and access regressions coexist with important gains, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
